Repositioning

Your company has changed. Has the way you’re seen?

Short answer

Repositioning is deciding how you want your company to be seen, by whom, and why, and then aligning everything you say and do with that decision. Established companies usually need it after growth, a change in direction, a merger, new leadership or a shift in market demand. It starts with the business, not the logo; a visual rebrand only helps once the position is clear.

Is this you?

  • The company has grown or changed direction, but its image hasn’t
  • Clients, partners or talent still meet an earlier version of you
  • You look modern and polished, but so does everyone around you
  • New leadership wants the market to see the company differently
  • You’re considering a rebrand, but aren’t sure what should change

Why it happens

A company’s image is set at a certain moment, and the company keeps moving. New services, new clients, new markets and new leadership change what the company is, while its message, materials and reputation stay where they were.

The gap grows quietly. By the time it is noticed, the market has already formed a view, and it is the old one.

Rebrand or reposition?

A rebrand changes how you look. Repositioning changes how you are understood. Most established companies need repositioning first: a clear decision about who they serve and what they want to be known for. If the visual identity then needs to change, that comes last.

How I work on this

  1. Listen: where the company is today, where it is going, and how leadership wants it to be seen
  2. Diagnose: how the market sees you now, and where that differs from who you have become
  3. Narrative: the new position and the story that carries it
  4. System: how the new position shows up across messaging, sales, channels, events and partners, so it is lived, not just announced

What you get

  • A clear position leadership can agree on and explain
  • A narrative that connects where you’ve been to where you’re going
  • A plan for rolling it out across every place the market meets you
  • A view on whether, and how much, the visual identity needs to change

FAQs

Will we need a new logo?

Not necessarily. Many repositioning projects need a clearer story far more than a new look. If the visual identity holds the company back, I’ll say so, and that change comes after the position is clear.

How do we avoid confusing existing clients?

A good repositioning tells existing clients a story that makes sense to them: how the company has grown and what that means for them. Planning that story is part of the work.
